title: Training and serving from the same facts
teaches: Feature stores: training and serving skew, point-in-time joins on availability time, offline and online stores, and logging against backfilling

blocks.text: When someone orders a meal through Uber Eats, the app shows an estimated delivery time before they pay, and a machine-learning model computes it. In September 2017 Jeremy Hermann and Mike Del Balso, engineers at Uber, described Michelangelo, the platform Uber had built over the previous two years to train and serve models like that one. Before Michelangelo, they wrote, teams built their own one-off systems, and a recurring difficulty was the data the models read.

The delivery-time model needs inputs such as the restaurant's average meal preparation time over the last hour, the same average over the last seven days, and the number of orders it has open. Those inputs, called **features**, were computed twice. For training, a data scientist wrote a batch query over months of historical orders in the data warehouse. For serving, an engineer wrote code in the production service that computed the same features from live data within milliseconds. The two pieces of code were written by different people in different languages against different data, and they drifted apart. A model that scored well in the team's offline tests then performed worse in production, and nothing was obviously broken.[^rules]

Michelangelo's answer was a shared **feature store**: a team defines a feature once, the platform computes it both for training and for serving from that one definition, and other teams can find and reuse it. In this lesson, we will design one. Our example is the routing team's arrival-time model from lesson M4, which reads features about every road segment on a route, such as its speed over the last 15 minutes and its usual speed at this hour, and which serves millions of predictions an hour.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** The feature store must let a team define a feature once, with its source, its computation and its owner. It must compute each feature over history for training and keep it current for serving, from the same definition. It must build training sets that give each example the feature values that serving would have had at that moment, serve the latest values to models within a few milliseconds, add a new feature over months of history, and record which feature versions each model was trained on.

**Non-functional.** Reading a request's features must take under 10 ms at the 99th percentile, at tens of thousands of requests a second. Streaming features must be no more than a minute or two old. A training set must be reproducible from its definition months later.
**Out of scope.** We will not design the models, the training jobs, or the streaming system that computes road speeds from phones, which lesson M4 covers.

parts.title: Skew, and where it comes from

blocks.text: **Training and serving skew** is any difference between the feature values a model was trained on and the values it receives in service. It has three common causes. The first is two implementations: the batch query and the service code compute "average speed over the last 15 minutes" slightly differently, one including stopped vehicles and one not. The second is defaults: when a value is missing, the training query fills in zero and the service fills in the road's speed limit. The third, and the hardest to see, is time: the training query gives an example a value that the service could not have known at that moment.

A feature store removes the first two causes by construction, because one definition and one implementation produce both sets of values, including the default for a missing value. The third cause needs a particular kind of join.

A training set is built by joining two things: **examples** (a trip requested at 12:30, which actually took 23 minutes) and the feature values that describe them. A naive join takes each feature's current value, or its value at the end of the day. That leaks the future into training: the 13:00 average speed for a road includes the congestion the 12:30 trip itself ran into, and the model learns to rely on information it will never have in service. A **point-in-time join** gives each example the value of each feature as of the example's time and no later.

"As of the example's time" needs care, because every feature value has two times attached to it. Its **event time** is the moment it describes: the average speed for the 15 minutes ending at 12:30. Its **availability time** is when the pipeline had finished computing it and the service could read it, perhaps 12:38 if the streaming job runs eight minutes behind. These are the two clocks of lesson 17. Serving at 12:30 can only read values available by 12:30, which describe 12:22 at best. A join on event time gives training the value about 12:30, which serving never has at 12:30. The correct join is on availability time.

blocks.caption: A road segment's speed over one hour, as computed for each moment and as the service could read it some minutes later. The training example is a trip requested at 12:30. Error figures are round numbers of our own.
blocks.task: Give training exactly what serving had, with a pipeline running several minutes behind

blocks.text: The latest-value join gives the best offline score of the three and the worst in service, which makes it dangerous: every offline test says the model is excellent. The event-time join is wrong by a smaller amount that grows with the pipeline's lag, and it is easy to build by accident, because the event time is the obvious timestamp to join on. Joining on availability time gives an offline score that predicts the real one, so the offline numbers in lesson P1's evaluation mean something.

Training and serving need the same values in very different shapes. Training reads millions of examples with the full history of each feature, in large sequential scans. Serving reads the latest value of a few hundred features for one request, in a few milliseconds. So a feature store has two stores, fed from one definition.

blocks.caption: A feature store: one definition, computed over history in batch and over new events as a stream, into an offline store for training and an online store for serving.

blocks.text: The **offline store** holds every value of every feature with its event time and availability time, in columnar files partitioned by date, the format the versioned datasets of lesson P3 use. Point-in-time joins run over it as batch jobs. The **online store** holds only the latest value of each feature for each key, such as a road segment's ID, in a key-value store like Bigtable (lesson 10) or Dynamo (lesson 12), so a lookup is one read by key. A batch job computes features that change slowly, such as the usual speed at each hour of the week, and writes to both stores. A streaming job computes features that change quickly, such as the speed over the last 15 minutes, writes the latest value to the online store, and appends every value it computes to the offline store, with both times, so training can later see exactly what serving saw.

The model and its features must also agree on versions. A model trained on version 3 of "speed over the last 15 minutes" must be served version 3, even after version 4 is defined, so the online store can hold both while models move across, and the model's metadata records which feature versions it needs, as the software and data versions on a vehicle must match in lesson D7.

At peak the routing service makes about 20,000 arrival-time predictions a second. A route crosses about 50 road segments, and the model reads four features for each, so each prediction needs about 200 feature values, and the service reads about 4 million values a second. If each value were a separate lookup, a request would fan out to many servers and wait for the slowest, the problem of lesson 9. The online store therefore keeps all of a segment's features in one row, the service reads the 50 rows of a route in one batched request, and the store's 99th-percentile latency must fit in the 10 ms that the service allows for features out of its 100 ms total.

The online store's size is set by keys, not history: 100 million road segments with a few hundred bytes of features each is tens of gigabytes, small enough to keep in memory across a modest cluster. The offline store grows with history: a value every minute for every busy segment, kept for two years, is hundreds of terabytes, which is why it lives in cheap columnar files.

When a team adds a new feature, it has no history, and a model cannot be trained on it until there are examples. There are two ways to get them, and they trade freshness against safety. **Logging** records the feature values that serving actually used, at the moment it used them, and trains on those logs. Logged values have no skew at all, since they are exactly what serving saw, but a new feature must be logged for weeks before there is enough to train on. **Backfilling** runs the new feature's definition over months of history in a batch job, producing a training set at once. It is fast, but the backfilled values come from the batch path and must be computed as of their availability times, which for a streaming feature means estimating how far behind the stream would have been.

Many teams do both: they backfill to start training at once, log from the day the feature goes live, and compare the logged values with the backfilled ones for the same days. A difference between the two is skew, found before the model ships rather than after. The same comparison, run continuously between a sample of logged serving values and the offline store, is the feature store's own health check.

Michelangelo's feature store held batch features computed with Hive and Spark and near-real-time features computed from Kafka streams, served from Cassandra, and let teams share features across models. Since then, feature stores have become a standard part of machine-learning platforms. Feast, released as open source by the Indonesian company Gojek and Google Cloud in 2019, provides the registry, the offline and online stores and the point-in-time join over storage a team already has. Airbnb built Zipline for the same purpose and in 2024 released its successor, Chronon, as open source with Stripe; Chronon's documentation describes its point-in-time joins as reproducing what was available online at each moment, the availability-time join above.

Most large cloud providers now offer a managed feature store. They differ in where they keep data and how they compute streaming features; the parts in this lesson, one definition, two stores, point-in-time joins and versioned features, are common to all of them.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **At ten times** (thousands of features across dozens of teams), the registry becomes the main product. Every feature has an owner, a freshness objective, a cost to compute and store, and a list of the models that read it, so features no model reads can be retired. Popular keys, such as the busiest road segments in a city at rush hour, become hot keys in the online store, and the store spreads them with replicas or a small cache in front, as in lesson 15.

**At a hundred times**, backfills of popular features take days and compete with everything else for the cluster, so they run at batch priority on spare capacity, as lesson D6's simulations do, and their results are cached by the feature's definition and the input versions, so two teams that backfill the same feature share one run. The comparison between logged and backfilled values runs on a sample of every feature every day, with alerts like those of lesson P4 when the two drift apart.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on giving training and serving the same facts
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A model scores much better in offline tests than in production. Its training set took each feature's value at the end of each day. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model is too small to learn the patterns that production data contains
Training saw values from after each example's time, information serving never has
Production traffic is busier than the training data, so the servers are slower
items.why: A value from the end of the day includes what happened after the example, so the model learns to rely on the future. A point-in-time join gives each example only what was known at its moment.

items.ask: A streaming feature describes the 15 minutes ending at 12:30 but is ready to read at 12:38. A training example is a trip requested at 12:30. Which value should the training join give it?
choices: The value describing the 15 minutes ending at 12:30, because that matches the trip's time
The newest value available to serving at 12:30, which describes a window ending before 12:30
The average of the values before and after 12:30, to smooth out the pipeline's lag
items.why: Serving at 12:30 can only read what the pipeline had finished by 12:30. Joining on availability time gives training exactly what serving will have; joining on event time gives it fresher data than serving ever gets.

items.ask: The training query fills a missing speed with 0, and the serving code fills it with the road's speed limit. What design removes this kind of skew?
choices: One feature definition, including its default, that computes values for both training and serving
A rule that every team reviews its serving code once a quarter
Removing every example with a missing value from training
items.why: Skew from two implementations disappears when there is only one. A feature store computes both paths from one definition, defaults included.

items.ask: Serving needs 200 feature values per prediction within 10 ms, at 20,000 predictions a second. Why not read them from the offline store?
choices: The offline store holds values in a different unit from the online store
The offline store is built for large scans of history; serving needs single-key lookups of the latest value in milliseconds
The offline store is only updated once a month, so its values are always out of date
items.why: Training and serving need the same values in different shapes. Columnar history files suit scans; a key-value store holding the latest value per key suits millisecond lookups.

items.ask: A team adds a new feature and wants to train on it this week. What are the choices, and their risks?
choices: Backfill it over history now, at the risk of skew if the backfill does not reproduce availability times; or log it from launch and wait weeks
Copy it from another team's model, which carries no risk because the feature is already used in production
Train without it this week and add it to the model's inputs in service, since the model will learn to use it there
items.why: Logging has no skew but no history; backfilling gives history at once but must reproduce what serving would have seen. Many teams do both and compare them for the same days.

items.ask: A model trained on version 3 of a feature is still in service when version 4, computed differently, is defined. What must the feature store do?
choices: Replace version 3 with version 4 everywhere, so all models get the improvement
Serve version 3 to the models that were trained on it until they are retrained, with each model recording the versions it needs
Refuse to define version 4 until every model has been retired
items.why: Giving a model a feature computed differently from its training data is skew. The store holds both versions while models move across, and each model's metadata names the versions it needs.

items.ask: During rush hour, the features for a city's ten busiest road segments are read thousands of times a second and one online store server is overloaded. What is the usual fix?
choices: Move those segments to the offline store, which has more capacity
Replicate those hot keys or cache them in front of the store, as for any hot key
Compute those segments' features less often, so there is less to read
items.why: Popular keys concentrate reads on one shard. Replicas or a small cache in front spread the load, the hot-key remedies of earlier lessons.

summary: **Skew is any difference between training and serving inputs.** It comes from two implementations, different defaults, or values the service could not have known in time.
**Define each feature once.** One definition, defaults included, computes values for both training and serving.
**Join on what was known, when.** A point-in-time join gives each example the feature values available to serving at its moment, never later ones.
**Availability time, not event time.** A value describing 12:30 that is ready at 12:38 was not available at 12:30; joining on event time trains the model on fresher data than it will get.
**Two stores, one definition.** Columnar history for training scans, a key-value store of latest values for millisecond lookups, both fed by the same batch and streaming jobs.
**Read a request's features in one batch.** Hundreds of values per prediction would otherwise fan out and wait for the slowest server.
**Log or backfill, and compare.** Logged values have no skew but no history; backfills give history at once; comparing them finds skew before the model ships.
**Version features with models.** A model is served the feature versions it was trained on until it is retrained.

rules.title: Train like you serve
rules.text: Martin Zinkevich's "Rules of Machine Learning", a widely read list of advice from Google engineers, gives the simplest defence against skew as its rule 29: record the features the model used in service, and train on those logs. Several neighbouring rules warn about skew from code that differs between the two paths.
